meta.title: Building a Full-Stack App with Agentic Engineering — Learning Notes
meta.desc: A principal engineer builds a full-stack iOS app from an empty terminal by talking to one orchestrator agent that delegates research, UX, backend, iOS and infra to parallel crewmates.

hero.kicker: L8 Principal · Kun Chen · learning notes
hero.title: Building a Full-Stack App with Agentic Engineering
hero.lede: A principal engineer builds a real full-stack iOS app — from empty terminal to working end-to-end — by talking to a single orchestrator agent and letting it delegate everything.

blocks.text:
- He builds **Eddie's Wallet**, a virtual-money allowance tracker for his son, with a parent mode and a read-only child mode.
- He talks to **one** agent (*First Mate*, the "captain → first mate" pattern). It spins up parallel *crewmates* for market research, tech research, UX, backend, iOS and infra.
- The whole build runs on an **efficient model (GPT-5.6 "Luna")**, not the top model — deliberately, to prove you don't need the best model for everything.
- Planning and review happen in **Lavish** — interactive HTML artifacts with editable decisions and diagrams — instead of reading walls of Markdown.
- The human's job shrinks to **judgment at decision points**: rejecting an over-priced hosting recommendation, cutting over-engineering, correcting spelling, approving secret access.
- Result: native iOS/iPad app + Fastify/Postgres backend on a **~$5/mo Hetzner VPS**, Apple Sign-In working, real data in the cloud, verified end-to-end in the simulator — ready for TestFlight.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.text: Get the *right thing* settled (market fit, requirements, architecture, cost) through cheap parallel research and interactive review — *then* let agents do the *thing right* (build, deploy, test) with the human only stepping in for judgment.

blocks.text:
**Kun Chen** — an L8 principal engineer who has worked at Meta, Microsoft and Atlassian — records his agentic-engineering workflow building a real project from scratch. This is the follow-up to an earlier workflow video that reached 600k views.

The project is **Eddie's Wallet**, an app his son asked him to build: a tracker for a child's allowance that today they manage on paper. The twist is that it should also *teach* basic financial concepts — balance, loans, credit cards, interest, repayment — introduced gradually and naturally.

blocks.title: Requirements he rambled up front
blocks.text: iOS-first (his son uses an iPad); a **parent mode** (deposit / manage / withdraw) and a read-only **child mode**; money is strictly **virtual**, never real; data is **cloud-persisted and portable** across his phone and the child's devices; and two kick-off tasks in parallel — *market research* (does this already exist?) and *technical research* (how do we build it full-stack?).

sections.title: The orchestration model
sections.intro: One captain, one first mate, many crewmates — the pattern that carries the whole session.

blocks.text:
Instead of managing many agents, Kun talks to exactly one: the **First Mate**. He is the "captain"; the first mate juggles everything and dispatches work to **crewmates** (sub-agents). This kills the two costs of multi-agent work — cognitive load and context-switching.

Crucially, each crewmate is a *normal agent in a normal terminal tab* (managed by **Herder**), so unlike hidden sub-agents in most harnesses, Kun can drop into any crewmate to observe or steer it — and First Mate tears the tab down automatically when a task finishes.

blocks.caption: Visualization 2 · Captain → First Mate → Crewmates
blocks.ascii:
Captain (you) — talks to only one agent · dumps thoughts
                    |
                    v
            First Mate — plans · delegates · always ready to talk
       /        |          |            |             \
Market scout  Technical  UX          Backend /      iOS app
(app exists?) scout      prototyper  infra          (SwiftUI,
-> report,    (stack,    (Lavish     (API·DB·VPS,   simulator)
then closes)  backlog,   wireframes) OpenTofu)
              docs)
   - - - crewmates report status back to First Mate (queued if busy) - - -

Why this beats normal sub-agents: each crewmate is a real agent in a real Herder tab —
observable and steerable. First Mate closes finished tabs automatically, persists task
state to files, and stays free to talk because it never does the heavy work itself.

blocks.title: Calm mode
blocks.text: In the PI agent, First Mate runs in *calm mode*: all the tool-call noise disappears, leaving only your prompt and First Mate's reply. Kun's take: with older, weaker models you needed to watch every tool call to steer; with today's models that's rarely necessary, so hiding the noise makes the experience clean.

sections.title: The toolchain

Orchestration          Herder · First Mate · PI agent · Calm mode · Server-side compaction

items.title: Herder
items.text: His "new tmux" — a terminal multiplexer that actually understands *agents*, not just shells and panes. Agent side-panel, quick-jump search, per-tab sessions.

items.title: First Mate
items.text: Open-source project by Kun. The single agent you talk to; delegates to crewmates so you avoid context-switching. Persists task state to files so compaction is safe.

items.title: PI agent
items.text: His favorite harness for running any non-Claude model. Hosts calm mode and extensions (Codex fast mode, OpenAI server-side compaction).

items.title: GPT-5.6 "Luna"
items.text: An efficient model run at x-high reasoning. Chosen deliberately over the best model to prove efficient models can carry a real build. Only stumbled once (VPS cost).

items.title: Lavish
items.text: Kun's tool that turns planning into interactive HTML artifacts — editable decisions, annotate-any-element feedback, and rendered architecture diagrams. Beats reading long Markdown.

items.title: Claude Design
items.text: Generates a full *design system* (not a one-off screen): brand, colors, icons, components, clickable screens — so future UI stays consistent. Ran on Sonnet.

items.title: Atomic Vault
items.text: Open-source secrets manager (by Homebrew's Max Howell). Per-access authorization dialog; the token is passed as an env var so the agent never sees plaintext. Safer than `.env` files.

items.title: No Mistakes
items.text: A local validation pipeline for every code change — the substitute for human review. Rule of thumb: turn it on for changes you'd otherwise have a human review. Off during prototyping.

items.title: OpenTofu
items.text: Declarative infrastructure: the machine and resources are all declared in an auditable, source-controlled file. Preferred over ad-hoc VPS setup.

items.title: Hetzner VPS
items.text: Low-cost host (~$5/mo) chosen over hosted Supabase (~$25+/mo) because the app has three users and no scale needs yet.

items.title: Cloudflare
items.text: Manages his domains/DNS. The agent used a vaulted API token to add a subdomain record pointing to the VPS and bring HTTPS up end-to-end.

items.title: Fastify + Postgres
items.text: The delivered stack: a Fastify API (session + wallet services), Apple as token issuer, Postgres holding the family ledger. Domain endpoints, not generic tables.

sections.title: Phase-by-phase walkthrough
sections.intro: The concise map above, expanded — what actually happened at each step.

items.title: 01 · Setup
items.text: Starts from an empty terminal with tools already installed. Launches Herder (session manager), clones and enters the First Mate repo, launches the PI agent, and deliberately switches from his usual GPT-5.6 to the more efficient **Luna** model — "I hope Luna doesn't backfire on me." First ground rule to First Mate: every task, every crewmate runs Luna at x-high reasoning. He also creates the local `eddies-wallet` repo with a dummy README and initial commit.

items.title: 02 · Kickoff ramble
items.text: Explains the whole product idea in one ~3,000-character stream of consciousness — the app, parent/child modes, virtual money, cloud persistence, iOS-first — and asks for two things in parallel: market research and technical planning. His deliberate style: "I just ramble… and let the agent figure things out."

items.title: 03 · Parallel research
items.text: First Mate spins up two crewmates in two tabs. The **market scout** finds no existing iOS app matching the full brief (virtual-only, parent-controlled, child read-only) and recommends building rather than installing an alternative. The **technical scout** builds a backlog, notes open decisions, and fetches Apple docs. Both confirmed running Luna as instructed.

items.title: 04 · Technical planning in Lavish
items.text: Rather than read a 351-line report, he asks for the review in Lavish. The scout recommends hosted Supabase; he pushes back on cost and puts a self-hosted VPS on the table, adding the auth story (Apple Sign-In now, Google later). He annotates the rendered architecture diagram directly — deleting over-engineered pieces like audit events and encrypted export to keep initial scope minimal.

items.title: 05 · Front-end prototyping
items.text: While the backend is being researched, he kicks off a parallel UX stream: clickable HTML wireframes in Lavish (not iOS code) for the key screens and user flow. He plays with them — family setup, device pairing, child read-only view, parent unlock — and gives feedback (use local currency not "tokens", remove a redundant "recent activity" button). Wireframes only; polish comes later.

items.title: 06 · Market inspiration → PRD → GitHub
items.text: He has First Mate mine the market research for concepts worth borrowing (money buckets, activity timeline, contextual lessons tied to real actions, gentle gamification — which he's wary of) and keep only what fits. Feedback is folded into a PRD written as the repo README, then committed and published as a **public GitHub repo** (he fixes a misspelling of "Eddie" both locally and on GitHub). Switches to a direct-PR workflow with First Mate auto-merging reviewed PRs.

items.title: 07 · Design system
items.text: Uses **Claude Design** to build a design *system* (for future consistency), pointed at the repo README. Opus is overloaded, so he tries Sonnet — "I also don't think the problem is too complex." Iterates: fixes uncentered text, and pushes hard on "this doesn't feel like a children's app" until it gets a friendlier, bouncy, piggy-bank feel. Also commissions app-icon options and exports the whole system as a zip.

items.title: 08 · Backend build (3 parallel streams)
items.text: First Mate creates three parallel work streams: backend API, DB schema/boundaries, and VPS foundation with backups + deployment automation. He redirects infra to use **OpenTofu** for declarative infrastructure, and grants Hetzner access via an **Atomic Vault** token — approving each production-secret access individually rather than blanket-allowing.

items.title: 09 · Apple Developer setup (browser automation)
items.text: He confirms a paid Apple developer membership and, instead of clicking through App Store Connect himself, tells First Mate to drive his real Chrome browser (via remote debugging / DevTools) to register the app ID and Sign-In capability. It hits a display-name validation error, he coaches it, and it succeeds on retry.

items.title: 10 · Integration & DNS
items.text: He supplies a Cloudflare API token (also vaulted) and a domain, and the agent adds a subdomain record pointing at the VPS, bringing the backend live over verified HTTPS. He splits repos: the iOS app stays in the open-source repo, the backend moves to a private one. Only one production environment — he cuts the agent's tendency to set up separate dev/prod tiers as over-engineering.

items.title: 11 · End-to-end testing & fixes
items.text: The iOS app was initially just a mock, so he pushes to real end-to-end integration: sign in with a real Apple account in the simulator and hit the real backend. The agent self-tests in the simulator, catches a wrong-address bug and an Apple AuthKit issue, and fixes them. He also has it neutralize the copy so "Eddie" isn't assumed to be every user's name. "Don't ask me unless there's something only I can do."

items.title: 12 · Architecture review & ship
items.text: While bugs are being fixed, he runs a backend architecture review in Lavish (endpoints, auth flow, DB schema) and finds nothing over-engineered. Final gate: he signs in with his real Apple account in the simulator, adds $10 in parent mode, sees it in the child view, signs out and back in — data persists from the cloud. It works end-to-end. Next step: a TestFlight build onto his son's iPad. All of it on Luna, with Sonnet for design.

sections.title: Backend architecture
sections.intro: What the agents actually built — reviewed (not hand-written) by Kun in Lavish.

blocks.text: "The phone is a client; Postgres is the referee." The iOS app keeps a local cache but authority lives on the server. Apple issues identity tokens; a session service exchanges them for a bearer session; a wallet service exposes narrow, domain-specific endpoints (not generic table access) backed by an immutable family ledger.

blocks.caption: Visualization 4 · Backend architecture & auth flow
blocks.ascii:
Apple — token issuer (identity)
   ^  identity token / verify issuer (dashed)
   |
iOS / iPad app ──HTTPS──> Fastify API (one production env) ──> Postgres — immutable family ledger
SwiftUI · local cache     ├ Session service — bearer / hash      parent_identities
native Sign in with Apple └ Wallet service — domain RPCs         sessions
                                                                 families → links parents ↔ children
                                                                 children · wallets
                                                                 loans
                                                                 ledger_entries (append-only)

blocks.title: Endpoints observed
blocks.text: Apple auth endpoints, plus `me`, `family`, `wallet`, and `child-view` — each rendering a specific screen's data. Kun's verdict on the whole thing: reasonable, nothing over-engineered.

sections.title: Where the human still steered
sections.intro: The workflow is agent-driven, but a handful of judgment calls were unmistakably human.

blocks.text:
- **Rejected the expensive recommendation.** The model pushed hosted Supabase at $25–40/mo based on wrong VPS cost data. Kun overrode from experience: a low-cost Hetzner VPS at ~$5/mo. "The only place Luna wasn't smart enough."
- **Cut over-engineering repeatedly.** Deleted audit events / encrypted export from the plan; refused separate dev/prod environments for a three-user MVP. GPT-5.6 "has a tendency to over-engineer."
- **Set scope boundaries.** Apple Sign-In now, Google later; wireframes not polish; no *No Mistakes* guardrail while there's no code to review.
- **Guarded production secrets.** Approved each Vault access individually rather than blanket-allowing, wanting to see every command touching Hetzner/Cloudflare.
- **Caught product/detail bugs.** Fixed the "Eddie" misspelling; flagged that "Eddie" shouldn't stand in for every user; chose USD over invented "tokens/points."
- **Pushed the agent to keep going.** "Don't ask me unless there's something only I can do" — agents are capable as long as they keep trying; they just need encouragement.

blocks.title: 1 · One agent to talk to
blocks.text: Delegating through a single First Mate removes cognitive load and context-switching. You dump thoughts; it figures out which crewmate to steer, when to spawn tabs, and when to close them.

blocks.title: 2 · Parallelize aggressively
blocks.text: Market + technical research, backend + frontend, three infra streams at once. "First Mate is always busy, not just sitting around." Prototype multiple things simultaneously to make fast progress on full-stack work.

blocks.title: 3 · You don't need the best model for everything
blocks.text: An efficient model (Luna) carried a real build end-to-end; Sonnet handled design when Opus was overloaded. Reserve the top models for genuinely hard problems.

blocks.title: 4 · Interactive planning beats walls of text
blocks.text: Lavish artifacts — editable decisions, annotate-any-element feedback, rendered diagrams — surface hidden requirements and are far easier to steer than a 351-line Markdown report.

blocks.title: 5 · Treat compaction as an implementation detail
blocks.text: Four auto-compactions, no visible loss — because OpenAI's server-side compaction is strong and First Mate persists task state to files. Let the agent run and compact; don't micromanage the context window.

blocks.title: 6 · Guardrails scale with delegation
blocks.text: As you hand agents more power, secrets management (Atomic Vault) and validation pipelines (No Mistakes) become more important, not less — you're no longer watching every tool call.

blocks.title: 7 · Infrastructure as code
blocks.text: Declarative OpenTofu config means the machine and resources are auditable, committable, and reproducible — not clicked together by hand.

blocks.title: Watch-outs he named
blocks.text: Efficient models can be wrong on facts (VPS pricing) and tend to over-engineer — keep human judgment at cost and scope decisions. Be deliberate about which changes need a review guardrail. And giving an agent your live browser/production secrets demands per-action approval.

blocks.text: The transcript below is **cleaned**: the auto-generated captions were fragmented, so sentences have been reconnected, filler removed, and obvious speech-to-text errors corrected (tool names especially). Meaning is preserved. Use the toggle to see the raw auto-generated captions.

blocks.title: Raw auto-generated captions
blocks.text: The raw auto-generated captions were the fragmented source for the cleaned transcript above (e.g. "Um so uh the first thing uh I will do uh with first mate..."). They have been reconnected into readable sentences with filler removed and tool names corrected. The full cleaned version is shown above; the original .txt caption file is the source.

"Hello everyone, my name is Kun. I worked at Meta, Microsoft and Atlassian as an L8 principal engineer. A few weeks ago I made a video about my agentic engineering workflow, which got 600,000 views. One of the most popular asks from that video was to make another one about me using my agentic engineering workflow to build a real project from scratch — and that's what we'll be doing today. Let's dive in."

"I'm starting from an empty terminal. My tools and environment are already set up, but I haven't created any project files yet, so I'll start with that. The first thing I'll do is launch Herder. Herder is kind of my new tmux — my replacement for it, and it's just better. It manages my agent sessions for me, and you'll see later why that gives me a really good experience. This is an empty session I just started."

"Next I'll set up First Mate. If you haven't heard of it, it's an open-source project I created that gained some popularity, which is nice. It's a new way of working that lets me — the captain — talk to only one agent, the first mate, and the first mate juggles everything for me. That really reduces my cognitive load and the burden of context-switching, so it makes my life a lot easier. Setup is easy: I clone the repo, go into it, and launch my agent there."

"Today I'll use the PI agent, because I want to use a GPT model and PI is my favorite harness for running any model that isn't Claude. My current model is GPT-5.6, and I use it a lot — but today I want to give myself a challenge and make this a bit more fun and uncertain, so I'm going to use Luna instead. A lot of the time we try to use the best model possible for everything because it gives better results, but I want to demonstrate that you don't really need the best model for everything — you can get a lot out of these more efficient models. I hope Luna doesn't backfire on me."

"My first instruction to First Mate is to lay down the ground rule that I want to use Luna: *Hey First Mate, let's set up a new project — a new local repo called Eddie's Wallet. Put a dummy README in it and make a commit to get it started. And lay down a ground rule: today every task, every crewmate is dispatched to a PI agent running GPT-5.6 Luna at x-high reasoning.*"

"First Mate runs a session-start script — it has scripts to handle the deterministic parts of running this whole thing, and it calls some skills. What I typically do is ignore all this noise, because it's just calling the tools and scripts it needs; I don't need to see which tools it called. So I have **calm mode** — it comes with First Mate and is only possible in the PI agent right now. When it's on, all that noise disappears and the terminal only shows my prompt and First Mate's response. With the weaker models we had a year or two ago it was really useful to watch what the agent was doing so you could steer it, but with today's models I rarely need to, so I hide the noise. First Mate reports: *Captain, Eddie's Wallet is set up.*"

"Now I'll tell First Mate what I really want to build — the same time I tell you: *This Eddie's Wallet project is an app my son Eddie asked me to build — an app for children to manage their allowances. Right now we write it in a notebook or just try to remember it, but it's hard to manage once there are a bunch of rules for how he earns and spends. I want it as a tracker for Eddie to manage his balance."*

"*I also want it to have educational value — to teach Eddie basic financial concepts like balance, loans, how credit cards work, making payments back on a loan, and interest on savings. The app should introduce these gradually, in a natural way kids can understand. It's iOS-only for now because Eddie mostly uses an iPad. I want a parent mode where I can deposit and manage withdrawals, and a child mode Eddie uses that's basically read-only — he can see his balance, whether he's taken a loan, and so on.*"

"*A few things I want done. First, market research — does an app like this already exist? If it does exactly what I described, I'll just install it; if not, that's a gap we can fill. Note the money must be virtual — it's just a virtual wallet tracking numbers, not real money. The data should be portable and stored in the cloud, because I may manage deposits from my phone while Eddie uses his iPad, and he switches between a Mac and an iPad. In parallel, look into the technical side: how would we build this full-stack, end to end? Kick off those two things in parallel.*"

"That was a long ramble — about 3,000 characters of requirements, ideas and thinking. This is typically how I kick off a new project: I ramble, explain everything on my mind to First Mate, and let the agent rationalize it. It's not showing me tool calls, which is nice; I can watch the token counter move to know it's working. I cap GPT context at 272K — there was a bug OpenAI reported where sending a request above that gets charged higher than usual, which is why people say Codex drains their quota — so I keep it at the safe cap."

"First Mate says both scouts are underway — it's already spun up two tabs: a market-research tab and a technical-research tab. This is how First Mate works: it doesn't try to do everything itself, because then it gets stuck doing one thing at a time. By dedicating tasks to crewmates, it gets a lot done in parallel. Both agents are confirmed running GPT-5.6 Luna at x-high, as asked."

"One thing that may be interesting: my quota. I have a little menu widget that tracks quota across Claude, Codex, a Kimi subscription — and I've already used up my Grok quota. Today we got a reset from Tibo, which is why I still have so much Codex quota. I'll also turn on fast mode with my Codex fast extension in PI — it turns out that affects all sessions, which is what I want. It costs more but lowers latency; I don't usually turn it on because GPT models are already fast, but it's better for a demo."

"The nice thing about First Mate and crewmates is that we can observe exactly what a crewmate is doing, because it's just a normal agent in a normal Herder tab — better than sub-agents in most harnesses, which are hard to see into or steer. I can drop into a crewmate session and talk to it if it's going wrong. The market-research agent is writing a report; the technical-research agent is building a backlog, noting which decisions are open for me to make later, and fetching Apple documentation because I asked for an iOS app. They're on the right track."

"Most of the time I don't even look at the crewmates — I just let First Mate juggle everything and only talk to First Mate. The market-research crewmate finished its report and reported back; First Mate rationalized it and tore down that agent's session automatically, because it's done. Before First Mate, I'd have created those tabs, tracked which agent was done, grabbed the report and closed the tab myself. Now First Mate does all of that."

"The market scout found no current iOS app matching the full brief — virtual-only money, parent-controlled, child read-only. The closest references are apps like a 'kiddo bank' that's web-only; different apps have different strengths but none do exactly what I described. I trust this because it clearly searched around. The recommendation is to prototype Eddie's Wallet rather than install a replacement. I agree — so there's value in building it."

"First Mate also closed the technical-research session and says it's done: it recommends a native SwiftUI iPad app, Supabase, Postgres with row-level security, an immutable server-side ledger, SwiftData local cache, no real-money integrations. I already have reactions. I don't really want to use Supabase — in my experience it gets expensive once you grow more complex — but this app doesn't have a single user yet besides Eddie, me and my wife, so it won't need scale; we can handle it ourselves without paying for SaaS. There's also quite a bit of ambiguity around identity and pairing."

"I don't want to read the report as a long wall of text, so I ask First Mate to review it with me in a better format — in **Lavish**: *I'm settled on the market research. Now let's discuss the technical research, especially the backend and database. Current recommendation is Supabase, but I don't want to jump to paying for SaaS. Another option I like is getting a VPS and self-hosting for now, especially with few users — put that on the table. If we self-host, we need an auth story: on iOS we'll support Sign in with Apple now, and Google sign-in later for a wider audience, but not today. Today is just Eddie's MVP. Come back with a technical proposal in Lavish, with all the open questions and decisions laid out.*"

"Lavish is a tool I built too — it uses HTML artifacts for better interaction on this kind of planning. That report.md is 351 lines; it's a lot of useful information but I don't like reading long walls of text, and it's hard to give feedback on specific parts. First Mate spins up another crewmate to do it — again, it delegates rather than doing it itself. Luna is doing a good job so far; nothing seems off."

"A Lavish artifact opens in my browser — the Lavish editor, which fixes layout issues before presenting, since generated artifacts sometimes have UI problems. The backend review's short version: 'buy operational simplicity before buying infrastructure.' It recommends hosted Supabase Pro, Apple now / Google later, virtual money only — those sound right — at about $25/month for MVP scale. $25 is still a lot for three users. It lists self-hosted VPS at roughly $30–60/month, which is wrong — it shouldn't cost that much; that's knowledge I have. The nice thing about Lavish is I can give feedback right on the artifact: I queue that this is wrong, that I've used Hetzner before and it offers a really low-cost VPS that can handle what we need, and that $25–40/month is way too expensive — a low-cost VPS should be around $5/month."

"It also drew an architecture diagram: 'the phone is a client, Postgres is the referee' — iPad app, local cache, native sign-in, retry/reconcile, narrow domain RPCs, membership checks in Postgres. On a high level that's fine, nothing controversial. But it baked in an immutable ledger with audit events, encrypted export — that's over-engineering; I don't need that, so I delete those annotations. Being able to see the architecture is really useful; otherwise we wouldn't have discovered those hidden requirements. On recovery: daily backup and nightly export is fine to start, but we'll revisit once we understand the real VPS cost. The parent should be able to set a PIN to gate parent-only actions. I send the whole artifact back to be revised on my feedback. This interactive back-and-forth is much friendlier than reading a wall of text and describing which part to change."

"While the backend is being researched, I think about what else we can do — the front end. *Hey First Mate, while the backend investigation is ongoing, let's prototype the front end. Give me a Lavish plan showing the potential user experience and journey — a bunch of prototypes of the key screens so I can get a feel for how they work, and I'll give feedback through the Lavish artifact.* First Mate spins up another tab for UX prototypes and comes right back to me — it's always ready to interact because it delegates everything."

"In parallel I also ask it to mine the market research for interesting concepts other products have that we might draw inspiration from. It suggests: a read-only kids view (I mentioned that); 'money buckets' — spend/save/give goals; a meaningful activity timeline; approval requests (withdrawals need parent approval — though this isn't real money, so they can propose actions); lessons attached to real actions (after a deposit, explain balance; before spending, explain trade-offs; when borrowing, explain principal) — that's exactly the educational aspect I wanted; a virtual loan simulator; flexible allowance rules (which we currently do manually); and gentle gamification — which I have mixed feelings about, because it engages kids but can feel manipulative — while avoiding heavy ads. The recommended inspiration mix — privacy, iPad-first, read-only child mode, family ledger, recurring allowance, contextual lessons — is good judgment: it only kept the things I also thought were relevant."

"Something came back on the backend, and Herder's agent side-panel shows all agents, their directory and which agent type — helpful when there are many. There's a keybind that brings up an agent-search pane to jump between sessions or search by title.
